questions.q: Why are Betti, de Rham, ℓ-adic, and crystalline cohomology often described as 'the same theory in different costumes'?
choices: They take values in the same target category
They produce numerically the same Betti numbers and satisfy parallel Künneth, Poincaré-duality, Lefschetz formulas
They are all defined for the same class of varieties using the same construction
questions.explain: They take values in genuinely different categories ($\mathbb{Q}$-vector spaces / filtered vector spaces / $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$-Galois reps / $\varphi$-modules), yet for any fixed $X$ they yield the same dimensions and satisfy the same formal identities — the unifying signal that motivates motives as their common source.

questions.q: The motivic functor $h\colon\mathsf{SmProj}_k\to\mathsf{Mot}_k$ is supposed to be 'universal' in the sense that:
choices: every cohomology functor on smooth projective varieties factors through $h$ (composed with a realization functor)
it sends every variety to a point
it is the unique additive functor on $\mathsf{SmProj}_k$
questions.explain: The defining property: realization functors $\mathsf{Mot}_k \to \mathcal{C}_R$ recover Betti / de Rham / ℓ-adic / crystalline by post-composing with $h$. Universality is on the realization side — every reasonable cohomology theory factors uniquely through the motivic data.

questions.q: Which of the following extra structures distinguish a *single* one of the four realizations from the other three?
choices: A Frobenius automorphism on a Witt-vector module
Eigenvalues of Frobenius pinned to absolute value $q^{i/2}$ on weight $i$
questions.explain: Galois action is special to ℓ-adic — none of the others carry a continuous $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ action. Frobenius-on-Witt-vectors is special to crystalline. The other two are not single-realization markers: every realization takes values in finite-dimensional vector spaces (Betti over $\mathbb{Q}$, dR over $k$, ℓ-adic over $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$, crystalline over $W(k)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$), and the Riemann hypothesis on Frobenius eigenvalues holds in *both* ℓ-adic and crystalline by Deligne / Katz–Messing, so it doesn't pick out one.

questions.q: An algebraic correspondence of degree $0$ from $X$ to $Y$ (smooth projective of dimensions $d_X, d_Y$) is an element of:
questions.explain: Correspondences live in $\mathrm{CH}^{d_X+r}(X\times Y)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ where $r$ is the degree; degree $0$ pins it to codimension equal to $\dim X$ in the product. The graph $\Gamma_f$ of any morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ is one canonical degree-$0$ class.

questions.q: Composition of correspondences $\beta\circ\alpha$ is defined as:
choices: $(p_{XZ})_*((p_{XY})^*\alpha\cdot(p_{YZ})^*\beta)$ on the triple product $X\times Y\times Z$
questions.explain: Composition pulls $\alpha$ and $\beta$ back to the triple product, intersects them, and pushes forward to $X\times Z$. The graph identity $\Gamma_g\circ\Gamma_f=\Gamma_{g\circ f}$ is the sanity check — composition of correspondences specialises to composition of morphisms via graphs.

questions.q: Which correspondence is the identity on the motive $h(X)$?
questions.explain: The diagonal $\Delta_X$, viewed in $\mathrm{Corr}^0(X,X)=\mathrm{CH}^{\dim X}(X\times X)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$, acts as the identity under composition. Its decomposition into Künneth components $\Delta = \sum \pi_i$ — when those components are algebraic — yields the projectors $(X,\pi_i)$ that split $h(X)$ by cohomological degree.

questions.q: An object of $\mathsf{Mot}_k^{\mathrm{Chow}}$ is which of the following data?
choices: a triple $(X, p, n)$ with $X$ smooth projective, $p\in\mathrm{Corr}^0(X,X)$ idempotent, and $n\in\mathbb{Z}$
questions.explain: After taking the pseudo-abelian envelope (to split idempotents) and inverting the Lefschetz motive (the $n$ Tate-twist parameter), motives are triples $(X,p,n)$. Plain varieties live inside as $(X,\Delta,0)$ — the diagonal projector and trivial twist.

questions.q: The motive of the projective line $\mathbb{P}^1$ decomposes as:
questions.explain: The diagonal $\Delta = e_0 + e_2$ where $e_0 = \mathbb{P}^1\times\{\mathrm{pt}\}$, $e_2 = \{\mathrm{pt}\}\times\mathbb{P}^1$ are orthogonal idempotents projecting onto $H^0$ and $H^2$. So $h(\mathbb{P}^1) = (\mathbb{P}^1,e_0,0)\oplus(\mathbb{P}^1,e_2,0) = \mathbf{1}\oplus\mathbb{L}$.

questions.q: Three flavors of pure motives — Chow, homological, numerical — differ in:
choices: the equivalence relation imposed on algebraic cycles in correspondence groups
the dimension of the varieties allowed
questions.explain: All three use $\mathrm{CH}^*(X\times Y)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ but quotient by different equivalence relations: rational (Chow, finest), homological (mod a chosen $H^*$), numerical (coarsest, two cycles equivalent if they intersect every other cycle the same number of times). Standard conjectures predict they collapse to one.

questions.q: Match the realization of $\mathbb{Q}(1)$ to its underlying object:
right: $\mathbb{Q}_p$ with Frobenius $\varphi$ acting by multiplication by $\frac{1}{p}$
$2\pi i \cdot \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{C}$ — a rank-1 $\mathbb{Q}$-Hodge structure of weight $-2$, type $(-1,-1)$
questions.explain: Each realization carries its own incarnation of $\mathbb{Q}(1)$ — Betti as $2\pi i\,\mathbb{Q}$, de Rham as a 1-dim space with shifted filtration, ℓ-adic as the cyclotomic character, crystalline as a $\varphi$-module with $\varphi = 1/p$. The fact that *all four objects describe the same motive* — and that $(2\pi i)^n$ is the period matrix tying Betti and de Rham — is the punchline of §4.

questions.q: In Betti realization, $\mathbb{Q}(1)$ is which Hodge structure?
questions.explain: $\mathbb{Q}(1)$ realizes as $2\pi i\cdot\mathbb{Q}\subset\mathbb{C}$, a rank-1 $\mathbb{Q}$-Hodge structure of weight $-2$ pure of Hodge type $(-1,-1)$. The shift to weight $-2$ is the source of the 'shift by $-2$ in cohomological degree' under Tate-twist.

questions.q: What controls multiple zeta values $\zeta(n_1,\ldots,n_r)$ from a motivic standpoint?
choices: the motivic Galois group of pure abelian varieties
the motivic Galois group of mixed Tate motives over $\mathbb{Z}$
no motivic structure — they are just analytic
questions.explain: Deligne–Goncharov–Brown: MZVs are periods of mixed Tate motives over $\mathbb{Z}$. The motivic Galois group of that subcategory acts on the periods; predicted relations among MZVs are reps-of-the-group statements. This is a rare case where the motivic framework is fully unconditional.

questions.q: A neutral Tannakian category over $k$ comes with a faithful exact tensor functor $\omega\colon\mathcal{T}\to\mathsf{Vect}_k$ (a fiber functor). Why is $\omega$ called 'neutral'?
choices: its image is the zero object
its target is just vector spaces over the base field $k$ (as opposed to a category of $L$-vector spaces for $L\supsetneq k$)
it is the identity on objects
questions.explain: 'Neutral' means the fiber functor lands in $\mathsf{Vect}_k$ over the very same field. Non-neutral Tannakian categories have a fiber functor only after extending scalars to a field $L\supsetneq k$ — and the resulting affine scheme is a torsor (gerbe) rather than a group.

questions.q: For a neutral Tannakian category $\mathcal{T}$ with fiber functor $\omega$, the Tannakian theorem identifies $\mathcal{T}$ with:
choices: $\mathsf{Rep}_k(G)$ for $G = \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega)$, the affine group scheme of tensor-automorphisms of $\omega$
questions.explain: $\mathcal{T}\simeq\mathsf{Rep}_k(G)$ where $G=\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega)$ encodes the natural tensor-automorphisms of $\omega$. The slogan 'a Tannakian category is the representations of an invisible group' is literal — the group is reconstructed from $(\mathcal{T},\omega)$.

questions.q: Match each Tannakian category with the group whose finite-dim representations it is equivalent to:
questions.explain: Each is a textbook Tannakian-category-with-named-group: Hodge structures see Mumford-Tate; Galois reps see the Galois group itself; regular $D$-modules see the differential Galois group. The motivic story is the union — one Tannakian category housing all three.

questions.q: Jannsen's theorem (1992) shows that — *unconditionally* — the category of numerical motives over $k$ is:
questions.explain: Jannsen proved $\mathsf{Mot}_k^{\mathrm{num}}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-linear, abelian, and semisimple — without any standard conjecture. Tannakianness on top of that requires the standard conjectures (so the category has a fiber functor compatible with the tensor structure).

questions.q: Modulo the standard conjectures, the motivic Galois group $G_{\mathrm{mot}}(k) = \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}^\otimes(\omega_B)$ is a:
choices: topological group with no algebraic structure
questions.explain: Pro-reductive (each finite-dim representation is semisimple) and pro-algebraic (limit of affine algebraic groups), reflecting that motives are pieces of varieties ranging over all dimensions. Classical $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ — a profinite group — is recovered as the étale-realization quotient of $G_{\mathrm{mot}}(\mathbb{Q})$.

questions.q: The Hodge realization gives a homomorphism $G_{\mathrm{mot}}(\mathbb{Q}) \twoheadrightarrow \mathrm{MT}(X)$. The Hodge conjecture is equivalent to which property of this map?
choices: surjectivity — i.e. every Hodge cycle on $X$ is algebraic
questions.explain: A Hodge cycle is a class in $H^{2p}(X;\mathbb{Q})$ of pure Hodge type $(p,p)$. The Hodge conjecture predicts every such class is the cycle class of an algebraic correspondence — i.e. comes from $\mathrm{CH}^p(X)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ via the cycle-class map. Equivalent reformulation in the Tannakian language: the Hodge realization $G_{\mathrm{mot}}(\mathbb{Q}) \to \mathrm{MT}(X)$ is *surjective* — the Mumford-Tate group is a literal quotient of the motivic Galois group, not a proper subquotient.

questions.q: Grothendieck's comparison theorem (1966) says that for $X$ smooth projective over a subfield $k\subset\mathbb{C}$:
choices: $H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/k)\otimes_k\mathbb{C} \cong H^*_B(X(\mathbb{C});\mathbb{C})$ — algebraic de Rham equals topological after tensoring with $\mathbb{C}$
questions.explain: After tensoring up to $\mathbb{C}$ — i.e. after evaluating both realizations at the same Hodge-de-Rham fiber functor — they become canonically isomorphic. Periods $(2\pi i)^n$ etc. record the discrepancy *before* tensoring, since the comparison is not defined over $\mathbb{Q}$.

questions.q: Fontaine's $p$-adic comparison theorem ties:
choices: $p$-adic étale and crystalline (via the period ring $B_{\mathrm{cris}}$)
questions.explain: The $p$-adic Hodge theory of Fontaine produces an isomorphism $B_{\mathrm{cris}}\otimes H^*_{\mathrm{cris}}(X_{\mathbb{F}_p}/W)\cong B_{\mathrm{cris}}\otimes H^*_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(X_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_p};\mathbb{Q}_p)$ for varieties of good reduction. This lets the $p$-adic Galois rep be read off the crystalline data.

questions.q: Artin's comparison theorem identifies which two realizations of a smooth projective variety $X / \mathbb{Q}$ after a base change?
choices: $\ell$-adic and crystalline via the period ring $B_{\mathrm{cris}}$
de Rham and crystalline via the de Rham–Witt complex
questions.explain: Artin's comparison: $H^*_B(X(\mathbb{C});\mathbb{Q}) \otimes_\mathbb{Q} \mathbb{Q}_\ell \cong H^*_{\text{ét}}(X_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}};\mathbb{Q}_\ell)$. Choice (A) is Grothendieck's comparison (Betti↔dR over $\mathbb{C}$). Choice (C) is Fontaine's $p$-adic comparison theorem (crystalline ↔ $p$-adic étale via $B_{\mathrm{cris}}$). Choice (D) is Bloch–Illusie / Berthelot–Ogus (de Rham–Witt). Each comparison theorem is a non-trivial bridge between two realizations of the *same* motive.

questions.q: The Lefschetz standard conjecture (B) asserts that:
choices: Hard Lefschetz holds for every smooth projective variety
the inverse of the Hard Lefschetz isomorphism $L^{n-i}\colon H^i\to H^{2n-i}$ is induced by an algebraic correspondence
every variety has an even Euler characteristic
questions.explain: Hard Lefschetz itself is a theorem (over $\mathbb{C}$); (B) asks that its inverse is algebraic — i.e. comes from a class in $\mathrm{CH}^*(X\times X)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$. (B) plus (C) imply numerical and homological equivalence agree, unblocking Tannakianness of $\mathsf{Mot}_k^{\mathrm{hom}}$.

questions.q: Voevodsky's triangulated category $\mathsf{DM}(k)$ functions as a substitute for the still-conjectural abelian category of mixed motives. What concrete role does it play in the proof of the Bloch–Kato conjecture?
choices: $\mathsf{DM}(k)$ collapses the standard conjectures to a single statement, which the proof verifies

Motivic cohomology $H^{p,q}_{\mathrm{mot}}(X;\mathbb{Z})$ is computed as $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf{DM}(k)}(M(X), \mathbb{Z}(q)[p])$ — a Hom-formula in $\mathsf{DM}(k)$ that turns Bloch–Kato (a statement about mod-$\ell$ Galois cohomology vs. Milnor K-theory) into a comparison of realization functors
$\mathsf{DM}(k)$ is equivalent to the category of Galois representations, reducing Bloch–Kato to a Galois computation
$\mathsf{DM}(k)$ is finite-dimensional, enabling a brute-force enumeration
questions.explain: The technical role of $\mathsf{DM}(k)$ in Voevodsky's program is the Hom-formula: motivic cohomology is intrinsically defined as Hom-groups in $\mathsf{DM}(k)$ between the motive $M(X)$ and Tate-twist shifts $\mathbb{Z}(q)[p]$. Bloch–Kato (Milnor K-theory mod $\ell$ ≅ Galois cohomology with $\mu_\ell^{\otimes *}$ coefficients) becomes a statement comparing two realizations of motivic cohomology: a Galois realization on one side, a Milnor-K realization on the other. The standard conjectures stay open.

questions.q: Which of the following is the *unconditionally true* version of the Tannakian motivic picture?
questions.explain: Mixed Tate motives over $\mathbb{Z}$ are fully constructed unconditionally and have an explicit motivic Galois group acting on multiple zeta values. The other two require some form of the standard conjectures (still open in general) to be Tannakian.
